## Conditions for ANOVA

As in the two-sample t-test, the ANOVA requires two conditions be met in order to trust the results of the test. 

### Normality Condition

- Let $\mu_j$ and $\sigma_j$ be the population average and standard deviation of Population $j$ for $j = 1, 2, \dots, g$. Assume that a simple random sample is taken from each population which follows a normal distribution $N(\mu, \sigma_i)$, and it is referred to as the **normality assumption**. Further assume that $\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2 = \dots = \sigma_g^2$, it is referred to as the **equal variance assumption**, and we simply denote the equal variance by $\sigma^2$. The normality and equal variance condition are graphically shown below for $g = 3$ groups.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.5, fig.width = 11, out.height = "100%", out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Three normal distributions"}
par( mfrow=c(1,2) )

### equal-variance assumption

mu = 90
sigma = 15
x.grid = seq( 45, 165, 0.01 )
plot( x.grid, dnorm(x.grid, mu, sigma), type="l", lty=1, axes=FALSE, xlab="", ylab="", main="Normality and Equal Variance condition" )

mu = 100
sigma = 15
lines( x.grid, dnorm(x.grid,mu,sigma), lty=2, col=2 )

mu = 110
sigma = 15
lines( x.grid, dnorm(x.grid,mu,sigma), lty=4, col=4 )

axis( 1, c( 0, 90, 100, 110, 200 ), labels=c("",expression(mu[1]),expression(mu[2]),expression(mu[3]),"") )
abline( h=0, col=8 )

abline( v=c(90,100,110), lty=c(1,2,4), col=c(1,2,4) )
legend( "topright", lty=c(1,2,4), col=c(1,2,4), legend=c("Population 1","Population 2","Population 3"), bty="n" )

### unequal-variance assumption

mu = 90
sigma = 7
x.grid = seq( 45, 165, 0.01 )
plot( x.grid, dnorm(x.grid, mu, sigma), type="l", lty=1, axes=FALSE, xlab="", ylab="", main="Normality and Unequal Variance condition" )

mu = 100
sigma = 11
lines( x.grid, dnorm(x.grid,mu,sigma), lty=2, col=2 )

mu = 110
sigma = 15
lines( x.grid, dnorm(x.grid,mu,sigma), lty=4, col=4 )

axis( 1, c( 0, 90, 100, 110, 200 ), labels=c("",expression(mu[1]),expression(mu[2]),expression(mu[3]),"") )
abline( h=0, col=8 )

abline( v=c(90,100,110), lty=c(1,2,4), col=c(1,2,4) )
legend( "topright", lty=c(1,2,4), col=c(1,2,4), legend=c("Population 1","Population 2","Population 3"), bty="n" )
```




## Case Study: Exam Scores and Seats

College students choose their seats in the classroom, and they tend to choose the same seat or nearby throughout the semester. A professor, who does not designate students' seats, hypothesized that their final exam scores differ by seating rows. The dataset $\texttt{seat.csv}$ is a sample of $m = 21$ students. The column $\texttt{score}$ is the final exam score of each student (numeric variable), and the column $\texttt{seat}$ is the student's seat ($\texttt{Front}$, $\texttt{Middle}$, and $\texttt{Back}$). The variable $\texttt{seat}$ can be treated as an ordinal categorical variable, and we can order the three levels using the $\texttt{factor}$ function. (Otherwise, it is ordered as $\texttt{Back}$, $\texttt{Front}$, and $\texttt{Middle}$ alphabetically.)

```{r, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.height = 4.5, fig.width = 5, out.height = "50%", out.width = "50%", fig.alt = "Boxplot of final exam score by seating row"}
library(mosaic)
examscore = read.csv("Data/seat.csv") ### read csv file
examscore ### print all rows
examscore$seat = factor(examscore$seat, levels = c("Front", "Middle", "Back"))
stats = favstats(score ~ seat, data = examscore) ### descriptive statistics
stats
boxplot(score ~ seat, data = examscore,
        horizontal = TRUE,
        main = "Final Exam Score by Seating Row",
        xlab = "Final Exam Score",
        ylab = "Seating Row",
        col = c(2, 3, 4) )
stripchart(score ~ seat, data = examscore,
           add = TRUE,
           method = "stack",
           pch = 19,
           offset = 0.2)
```

### Hypotheses

Let $\mu_1$, $\mu_2$, and $\mu_3$ be the unknown expected eaxm score for $\texttt{Front}$, $\texttt{Middle}$, and $\texttt{Back}$, respectively. Our goal is to test for the null hypothesis $H_0$: $\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \mu_3$ (i.e., the expected exam score is the same between the three seating rows) versus the alternative hypothesis is $H_1$: $\mu_1 \ne \mu_2$, $\mu_1 \ne \mu_3$, or $\mu_2 \ne \mu_3$ (i.e., at least one seating row has a different expected exam score) at a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$.

### ANOVA

The sample sizes are $n_1 = 7$, $n_2 = 8$, and $n_3 = 6$ for $\texttt{Front}$, $\texttt{Middle}$, and $\texttt{Back}$, respectively. The sample means are $\bar{X}_1 = 89.29$, $\bar{X}_2 = 81.75$, and $\bar{X}_3 = 77.83$, and the sample standard deviations are $S_1 = 6.626$, $S_2 = 7.686$, and $S_3 = 8.909$. It appears that students in $\texttt{Middle}$ scored slightly higher than in $\texttt{Back}$ by 3.92 points on average, and students in $\texttt{Front}$ scored substantially higher than in $\texttt{Middle}$ by 7.54 points on average. The variance of exam scores by are similar among the three groups (sample standard deviations are similar).

Below is the calculation of F statistic and p-value in a naive way.

```{r}
( overall_mean = mean(examscore$score) ) ### overall sample mean
( group_mean = stats$mean ) ### group sample means
( group_sd = stats$sd ) ### group sample standard deviations
( group_size = stats$n ) ### group sample size
( m = sum(group_size) ) ### total sample size
( g = length(group_size) ) ### number of groups
( ssw = sum( (group_size - 1) * group_sd ^ 2 ) ) ### within-group sum of squares
( dfw = m - g ) ### within-group degrees of freedom 
( msw = ssw / dfw ) ### within-group mean square
( ssb = sum( group_size * (group_mean - overall_mean) ^ 2 ) ) ### between-group sum of squares
( dfb = g - 1 ) ### between-group degrees of freedom
( msb = ssb / dfb ) ### between-group mean square
( f = msb / msw ) ### F statistic
( p = 1 - pf( f, dfb, dfw ) ) ### p-value

```

This long calculation can be done using the $\texttt{aov}$ function, and the ANOVA table can be printed using the $\texttt{anova}$ function.

```{r}
fit = aov(score ~ seat, data = examscore) ### ANOVA calculations
anova(fit) ### print ANOVA table
```

The calculated test statistic is F = 3.6718, and the p-value if p = 0.043 which is less than $\alpha = 0.05$. At a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$, the sample of 21 students (7 in $\texttt{Front}$, 8 in $\texttt{Middle}$, and 6 in $\texttt{Back}$) provides significant evidence for the difference in the expected exam score between the three groups (F = 3.6718\$, $\nu_b = 2$, $\nu_w = 18$, and p = 0.043).

### Equal Variance Assumption

The population variances $\sigma_1^2$, $\sigma_2^2$, and $\sigma_3^2$ can be estimated by the sample variances $S_1^2$, $S_2^2$, and $S_3^2$, respectively. As a **simple rule of thumb of checking equal variance assumption**, if the largest sample variance is not greater than four times of the smallest sample variance, it is considered as no strong sign of violating equal variance assumption. In this sample, $\frac{(8.9088)^2}{(6.6261)^2} = 1.8$, so the equal variance assumption is good.

As in the two-sample t-test, it can be formally assessed by the Bartlett test.

```{r}
bartlett.test(score ~ seat, data = examscore)$p.value
```

The Bartlett test results in p = 0.8 (greater than $\alpha = 0.05$), so there is no sign of violating the equal variance assumption.

### Normality Assumption

The group sample mean is referred to as the **fitted value** (or **predicted value**) and individual student's score is referred to as the **observed value**. The difference between observed value and fitted value (observed minus fitted) is referred to as the **residual**.

```{r}
fit = aov(score ~ seat, data = examscore)
rslt = data.frame( observed = examscore$score,
                   group = examscore$seat,
                   fitted = fit$fitted.values,
                   residual = fit$residuals )
rslt
```

The third student who scored 100 is 10.7 points above the fitted value (group sample average), and the sixth student who scored 79 is 10.3 points below the fitted value. The residuals are natural deviations from the group average, and the normality assumption can be checked using the Q-Q plot and Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals.

```{r, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 5, out.height = "50%", out.width = "50%", fig.alt = "Q-Q plot of residuals of exam scores"}
qqnorm(fit$residuals, main = "Q-Q Plot of Residuals")
qqline(fit$residuals)
shapiro.test(fit$residuals)$p.value
```

The Q-Q plot is fairly straight, and the Shapiro-Wilk results in p = 0.636 (greater than $\alpha = 0.05$), so there is no sign of violating the normality assumption.

Since both normality assumption and equal variance assumptions are satisfied, the conclusion of $H_1$ in the ANOVA test is valid.










For the purpose of demonstration, suppose we want to compare three averages $\mu_1$, $\mu_2$, and $\mu_3$. The conclusion of ANOVA is either $H_0$: $\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \mu_3$ or $H_1$: $\mu_1 \ne \mu_2$, $\mu_1 \ne \mu_3$, or $\mu_2 \ne \mu_3$. If $H_1$ is concluded at a significance level of $\alpha$, it does not specify which pairwise difference(s) are statistically significant. The Tukey's method (also known as the Tukey's honest significant differences) is a **post-hoc test** (identifying significant pairwise difference(s)) when the conclusion of ANOVA is $H_1$.

## Family-wise Confidence Level

A general form of a confidence interval (CI) for any unknown parameter is

$$
\texttt{point} \,\, \texttt{estimate} \,\, \pm \,\, c \times \texttt{SE} 
$$ {#eq-ci}

where $c$ is the critical value which reflects a confidence level $1 - \alpha$ and $\texttt{SE}$ is the standard error which quantifies the uncertainty about point estimation. If a CI for $\mu_j - \mu_k$ does not include zero at a confidence level of $1 - \alpha$, it is equivalent to concluding $\mu_j - \mu_k \ne 0$ (a two-sided test) at a significance level of $\alpha$. It is a natural idea to build three 95% CIs, one for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$, one for $\mu_1 - \mu_3$, and one for $\mu_2 - \mu_3$, and determine which pairwise difference(s) are statistically significant.

Here is a challenge. When there are three independent CIs for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$, $\mu_1 - \mu_3$, and $\mu_2 - \mu_3$, where each CI captures the true value of $\mu_j - \mu_k$ with a probability of 0.95, all three independent CIs capture the true values of $\mu_1 - \mu_2$, $\mu_1 - \mu_3$, and $\mu_2 - \mu_3$ with a probability of $(0.95)^3 = 0.857$. In this case, we say that we have a family-wise confidence level of 0.857. In general, a **family-wise confidence level** is the probability that all CIs capture the true parameter values. If we want a family-wise confidence level of 0.95, the confidence level for each individual CI should be $(0.95)^{1/3} = 0.983$. In general, when we want $k$ independent CIs at a family-wise confidence level of $1 - \alpha$, each confidence interval should have a confidence level of $(1 - \alpha)^{1/k}$. This method is known as the **Sidak's method**.

This method is brilliant, but there are two caveats. The first caveat is that CIs for multiple pairwise differences are not independent. The second caveat, which follows from the first caveat, is that Sidak's method is conservative. In other words, it results in long CIs (imprecise interval estimation).

## Tukey's Honestly Significance Difference (HSD)

John Tukey (1915-2000), an American mathematician and statistician, suggested a method of accurately calculating the critical value $c$ and the standard error $\texttt{SE}$ in @eq-ci. The formula of $c$ is complicated, but $c$ can be calculated by $\texttt{qtukey}( 1 - \alpha, \, \texttt{nmeans} = g, \, \texttt{df} = \nu_w ) \, / \, \texttt{sqrt}(2)$ where $1 - \alpha$ is a fixed family-wise confidence level, $g$ is the number of groups, and $\nu_w = m - g$ is the within-group degrees of freedom ($m$ is the total sample size). The standard error is estimated as

$$
\texttt{SE} = \sqrt{ \texttt{MSW} \left( \frac{1}{n_j} + \frac{1}{n_k} \right) }
$$

where $\texttt{MSW}$ is the within-group mean square (from the ANOVA table) and $n_j$ and $n_k$ are the sample sizes in group $j$ and $k$, respectively. This method is known as the **Tukey's method** or **Tukey's honestly significant difference** **(HSD)**.

**Note:** As the ANOVA test, the Tukey's HSD is valid under the normality and equal variance assumptions.

Let us apply the Tukey's HSD to $\texttt{seat.csv}$. Let $\mu_1$, $\mu_2$, and $\mu_3$ be the unknown expected exam score for $\texttt{Front}$, $\texttt{Middle}$, and $\texttt{Back}$, respectively. Below are the descriptive statistics, ANOVA table, and critical value.

```{r, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
library(mosaic)
examscore = read.csv("Data/seat.csv") ### read csv file
dim(examscore) ### dimension of data
table(examscore$seat) ### sample size by seat
examscore$seat = factor(examscore$seat, levels = c("Front", "Middle", "Back"))
stats = favstats(score ~ seat, data = examscore) ### descriptive statistics
stats
fit = aov(score ~ seat, data = examscore) ### ANOVA
anova(fit)
c = qtukey(0.95, nmeans = 3, df = 18) / sqrt(2) ### critical value
c
```

At a family-wise confidence level of 0.95, Tukey's CIs for $\mu_2 - \mu_1$, $\mu_3 - \mu_1$, and $\mu_3 - \mu_2$ can be calculated as follows:

- CI for $\mu_2 - \mu_1$: $(81.750 - 89.286) \, \pm \, 2.552 \sqrt{59.653 \left( \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{7} \right) }$

- CI for $\mu_3 - \mu_1$: $(77.833 - 89.286) \, \pm \, 2.552 \sqrt{59.653 \left( \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{7} \right) }$

- CI for $\mu_3 - \mu_2$: $(77.833 - 81.759) \, \pm \, 2.552 \sqrt{59.653 \left( \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{8} \right) }$

The above calculations can be done using the $\texttt{TukeyHSD}$ function in R (after the ANOVA test).

```{r, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 6, out.height = "50%", out.width = "50%", fig.alt = "Tukey's CIs"}
hsd = TukeyHSD(fit)
hsd
plot(hsd)
```

Resulting Tukey's 95% family-wise CIs are $(-17.7, +2.7)$ for $\mu_2 - \mu_1$ ($\texttt{Middle} - \texttt{Front}$), $(-22.4, -0.5)$ for $\mu_3 - \mu_1$ ($\texttt{Back} - \texttt{Front}$), and $(-14.6, +6.7)$ for $\mu_3 - \mu_2$ ($\texttt{Back} - \texttt{Middle}$). The CI for $\mu_3 - \mu_2$, which does not including zero, is the only significant different. We conclude that the expected score of students seating in the back row is lower than of students seating in the front row (p = 0.039), and at a family-wise confidence level of 0.95, we estimate that the difference in the expected exam score between back row and front row is between –22.4 and –0.5.

The below table compares Tukey's 95% family-wise CIs and Sidak's 95% family-wise CIs for $\mu_2 - \mu_1$, $\mu_3 - \mu_1$, and $\mu_3 - \mu_2$. As aforementioned, the Sidak's method is conservative, resulting in longer CIs than the Tukey's method, and none of the pairwise differences is statistically significant (including zero).

| Parameter | Tukey's CIs | Sidak's CIs |
|:----------------------:|:----------------------:|:----------------------:|
| $\mu_2 - \mu_1$ ($\texttt{Middle} - \texttt{Front}$) | $(-17.7, +2.7)$ | $(-18.5, +3.4)$ |
| $\mu_3 - \mu_1$ ($\texttt{Back} - \texttt{Front}$) | $(-22.4, -0.5)$ | $(-23.5, +0.6)$ |
| $\mu_3 - \mu_2$ ($\texttt{Back} - \texttt{Middle}$) | $(-14.6, +6.7)$ | $(-15.5, +7.6)$ |

: Tukey's 95% family-wise CIs and Sidak's 95% family-wise CIs for the three pairwise differences

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = FALSE}
msw = as.numeric( unlist( anova(fit) )[6] )
xbar = stats$mean
point21 = xbar[2] - xbar[1]
point31 = xbar[3] - xbar[1]
point32 = xbar[3] - xbar[2]
n = stats$n
g = length(n)
conf_level = (0.95) ^ (1/g)
alpha = 1 - conf_level
c21 = qt( 1 - alpha / 2, n[2] + n[1] - 2 )
c31 = qt( 1 - alpha / 2, n[3] + n[1] - 2 )
c32 = qt( 1 - alpha / 2, n[3] + n[2] - 2 )
se21 = sqrt( msw * ( 1/n[2] + 1/n[1] ) )
se31 = sqrt( msw * ( 1/n[3] + 1/n[1] ) )
se32 = sqrt( msw * ( 1/n[3] + 1/n[2] ) )
round( point21 + c(-1, 1) * c21 * se21, 1 )
round( point31 + c(-1, 1) * c31 * se31, 1 )
round( point32 + c(-1, 1) * c32 * se32, 1 )

```

**Problem 1.** Fill in the blank. Be cautious that some words have hyphen (-) as joint words.

a\. The \[...\] variance refers to the variability of individual data points from their own group sample average.

b\. The \[...\] variance refers to the variability among the group sample averages.

c\. The normality assumption implies that a \[s... r... s...\] is observed from a normal distribution for each group.

**Problem 1.** Exercise scientists believe that maximum speed (km/h) is an indicator of athletes' physical strength and speed, and it is an important physical ability for team sports played in a field like soccer. Do players have different maximum speed by position, on average? To address this question, let us use the dataset $\texttt{Euro.csv}$, focus on the most recent competition (Euro 2024), and compare the maximum speed of $\texttt{Defender}$, $\texttt{Foward}$, and $\texttt{Midfielder}$ (remove $\texttt{Goalkeeper}$) using the ANOVA. The following code cleans the original data for our objective. Study the code.

```{r, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
library(mosaic)
euro = read.csv("Data/Euro.csv") ### read data
head(euro, 5)
dim(euro) ### dimension of data
table(euro$Event) ### count by competition
table(euro$Position) ### count by position
euro2024 = subset(euro, Event == "Euro 2024" & Position != "Goalkeeper") ### subset 493 players played in Euro 2024
dim(euro2024) ### dimention of subsetted data
table(euro2024$Position) ### count by position
```

Let $\mu_1$, $\mu_2$, and $\mu_3$ (parameters of interest) denote the expected maximum speed of $\texttt{Defender}$, $\texttt{Foward}$, and $\texttt{Midfielder}$ among European players in 2024 (population of interest). Answer the following question based on the cleaned data frame $\texttt{euro2024}$.
